title: Have Your Feelings (Or They Will Have You)
coreMove: Translate a vague or disguised feeling into a direct report you can own.
sourcePressure: The chapter says feelings are already in the room and teaches how to name them accurately without turning them into accusations.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Dumping emotion or suppressing it in the name of professionalism.

sourceAnchors.name: Have your feelings or they will have you
sourceAnchors.detail: The source's chapter phrase captures the mechanism: unexpressed feelings redirect into tone, contempt, avoidance, and escalation.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The feeling you refuse to name keeps speaking anyway, usually through the sentence you thought was neutral.

sourceAnchorsNote: No chapter-specific real named anecdote, study, or researcher was available in the source sidecars for this chapter. Source anchors are traceable framework artifacts or edition/context facts only; do not invent named studies or reuse the source-banned Jack-Michael, Sydney, or author-family examples.

hook: Do not open ch05 with a generic dread-before-meeting frame
Do not begin with a definition of the chapter term

counterintuition: Avoid the shell 'you think X, but actually Y'

examples: Avoid repeated coffee-table, classroom, narrow-kitchen, bus-depot, marker, mug, or radiator shells
Avoid six workplace meetings with changed names
Avoid making every case a manager feedback scene

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: use these six opening devices in order: sensory detail first; second-person You direct address; dialogue first line; environmental detail before any human; retrospective first line; timestamp+name+action
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of timestamp plus named protagonist plus prop plus decision that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps
